 It weighs nearly 2 pounds and was picked up on a salt plain in Mali. A NASA-funded study now shows it is one of the oldest pieces of Mars ever found on Earth, and the first from a part of the planet never sampled before. 
 In 2022, a rose-colored stone weighing about 800 grams, nearly 2 pounds, was found in the Sahara, on the Teghaza salt plain in Mali. It now carries the name of that place: Teghaza 001. According to NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory , it is not an ordinary desert rock. It came from Mars.
 In short 
 Teghaza 001, a meteorite found in Mali in 2022, comes from the crust of Mars.
 Water altered its rock about 4.1 billion years ago, which makes it one of the three oldest Martian meteorites known on Earth.
 According to the researchers, it is the first sample from a region of Mars never sampled before.
 How scientists know it came from Mars
 Researchers at the University of New Mexico compared the oxygen isotopes in the rock with those of other Martian meteorites and found a match, JPL explains. Its minerals and chemistry also match data gathered by NASA’s Mars missions. According to CBS News , its zircon-bearing volcanic minerals resemble rocks seen by the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in the planet’s southern highlands. It joins a small club: about 435 Martian meteorites are known, CBS reports. Each of them was blasted off Mars by an impact before eventually falling to Earth.
 A sample smaller than a fingernail
 The main study, led by Yang Liu of JPL, appeared in the journal Science . To date the rock, the team, which included Caltech geochemist Francois Tissot, applied an age-dating method to a sample smaller than a fingernail, according to CBS. The results show that water altered the rock about 4.1 billion years ago, and the rock itself may be even older. A separate paper published in June in Science Advances looked at the water it contains.
 “It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique,” Liu said in the JPL announcement. Lee Saper, formerly at JPL and now at NASA’s Ames Research Center, added: “This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before.” According to CBS, Liu described the meteorite as a “Rosetta Stone for Mars,” a phrase Liu attributed to one of the paper’s reviewers.
 The limit
 A meteorite only tells us indirectly where it came from on Mars. The link with the southern highlands rests on mineral similarities with rocks seen from orbit, not on an identified launch site. The age of 4.1 billion years refers to the moment water altered the rock, so its formation may be older still. The published accounts also do not say who found the stone or how long it had been lying in the desert. The team now hopes, in Tissot’s words, “to pave the way for dating even more Martian meteorites.”
 Rocks from space keep surprising the people who handle them. In Spain, two pieces of a Bronze Age treasure turned out to be made of metal from space . On Mars itself, the Curiosity rover cracked open a rock full of yellow sulfur crystals . Teghaza 001 brings a piece of the planet’s ancient crust straight to our labs.
